title: A long licensed case: eight exhibits, four voices, two dated revisions
why: What a business school case actually looks like when it is pasted whole: exhibits, memo dates, a superseded number and four people who disagree. The step-2 prompt gets a brief written from all of it, and the rules that bite here are the ones about the Evidence Room — 6 to 12 documents, three roles present, every stakeholder documented — which a long input can satisfy by copying and must instead satisfy by re-skinning.
licenseTerms: Licensed for adaptation and classroom distribution; the publisher's name must appear in the seed record and the adapted text must not reproduce the exhibits verbatim.
seedText:
Calderwood Instruments (A): the service-contract renewal.

Calderwood Instruments assembles benchtop spectrometers for university and hospital laboratories. Revenue in the year to March was 84 million dollars, of which 31 million came from service contracts sold alongside the instruments. The service business has been managed as an attachment to the hardware sale for eleven years, and in that time its price has moved once.

In January the commercial director, Helene Ferrand, proposed moving the standard service contract from a flat 4,200 dollars a year to a tiered structure: 3,200 dollars for a response-within-five-days tier, 5,600 dollars for next-day, and a 9,400 dollar tier including consumables. Her deck put the contribution margin on the next-day tier at 61 percent and the incremental margin from the move at 2.4 million dollars in the first full year.

Exhibit 1 (January deck, page 4) shows the 61 percent figure. The footnote says it excludes the cost of the field engineers' travel, which the service operations lead, Marcus Okonjo, has argued for two years should be charged to the contract rather than to overhead. Exhibit 4, a costing note dated 12 March, allocates travel at 780 dollars per next-day call-out and puts the next-day contribution margin at 44 percent. Nobody has restated the 2.4 million dollar figure on the March basis.

Exhibit 2 is a customer survey run in November. Of 340 contract holders, 118 responded; 61 percent of respondents said they would pay more for a next-day guarantee. The survey was sent to contacts on the service mailing list, which is maintained from support tickets. The head of customer research noted in an appendix that the list is weighted toward accounts that have had an instrument fail in the last eighteen months.

Exhibit 3 is a cohort table of contract renewals by year of instrument purchase. Instruments bought in the two years after a price rise renew their contracts at 71 percent; instruments bought in other years renew at 88 percent. The table covers seven cohorts and the difference holds in six of them.

Exhibit 5 is a capacity note from the field service manager, Anne-Sophie Baptiste. Next-day response across the current installed base would require either four additional engineers at a fully loaded 96,000 dollars each, or a regional depot model that reduces travel but adds a 340,000 dollar fit-out. Neither is in the January deck.

Exhibit 6 is a one-page competitor scan. Two of the four named competitors publish tiered service pricing; one of the two withdrew its cheapest tier in the year after introducing it, and the scan does not say why.

At the April board meeting the chief executive asked for a recommendation on the tier structure, the price of each tier, and the first-year margin the board should expect. The board has said it will not approve additional headcount in the same meeting as a price change.

The finance director's note of 19 March, circulated after Exhibit 4, says: 'The January margin numbers are superseded. Any recommendation put to the board must be stated on the March costing basis or it is not a number the board can act on.'
